stories.topic: Bowling Rahul Dravid with an office cricket ball
stories.summary: While Amit was managing editor at Cricinfo, Rahul Dravid visited the office. The staff played office cricket with a ball halfway between a squeezy ball and a plastic ball, which could be given forward or backward spin to make it zip through the air. Amit talked Dravid into batting against him. His first ball was a wide, and Dravid was clean bowled by each of the next two. Dravid threw the bat away and said he was done.
stories.insight: The story came up when Ajay asked Amit for his 'thought-to-action ratio' in each sport he loves. Amit's only win as a cricketer came with a trick ball in an office, which makes his point for him: his love of sport is mostly that of a thinker and watcher, and that is the spirit of this episode.
stories.quote: I convinced Rahul to bat while I bowl to him. And my first ball was a wide. Didn't work out. He was clean bowled off the next two balls. And then he said, Fuck you, Shoaib Akhtar, I'm not playing with you. And he threw the bat away.

stories.topic: The cycling fan who can't ride a cycle
stories.summary: Amit admits that his thought-to-action ratio for cycling is zero because he never learned to ride one. He blames a privileged childhood, with a father in the IAS and a car always available, and then a working life in Bombay spent on local trains and buses before he bought a car. He used to be embarrassed about it and no longer is. His passion is purely intellectual and built on watching a great deal of racing.
stories.insight: Expertise as a spectator is a real kind of expertise. Ajay's line that 'you don't have to be a hen to know about eggs' turns Amit's handicap into a vantage point.
stories.quote: I don't know how to ride a cycle. Which I used to be very embarrassed about, but now I'm like whatever.

stories.topic: Oscar Pereiro, the accidental Tour de France champion
stories.summary: In a mid-2000s Tour de France (Amit wasn't sure of the year), the GC favourites let a breakaway go that included Oscar Pereiro, who wasn't considered a real contender. He took the overall lead for a while, and the favourites didn't care. They were busy fighting one another and Floyd Landis. Pereiro finished second. When Landis was disqualified for drug use, Pereiro became Tour de France champion.
stories.insight: GC teams decide which breakaways are harmless, and those calculations can go badly wrong. If every rival watches only the others, an ignored outsider can slip through. In cycling, a doping disqualification can then turn second place into the title.
stories.quote: So there is, you know, one Tour de France champion who was a lucky beneficiary.

stories.topic: Tour of Flanders 2022: Pogacar plays cat-and-mouse and finishes fourth
stories.summary: Tadej Pogacar, 65 kg and a superb climber, attacked out of an already select group. Only Mathieu van der Poel, 75 kg and the faster sprinter, hung on over the hills. On the flat run-in Pogacar knew he would lose a sprint from the front, so he slowed almost to a standstill to make van der Poel lead. Van der Poel slowed too. Meanwhile three chasers, who knew they couldn't win and so had every reason to cooperate, rode flat out and caught them. Van der Poel won the sprint, Dylan van Baarle was second, Valentin Madouas third, and Pogacar, who had dominated the race, finished fourth.
stories.insight: In a stand-off, the cost of waiting can be someone else arriving. By optimising for the one-on-one sprint, Pogacar let a third party back into the race, and in that group he was the weakest sprinter.
stories.quote: Pogacar ends up fourth because he waited too long and the other guys caught up and then he's the worst sprinter of the bunch.

stories.topic: Paris-Roubaix: van Aert caught in a two-against-one trap
stories.summary: In last year's Paris-Roubaix, three riders were heading for the finish together: Mathieu van der Poel, his great rival Wout van Aert, and van der Poel's teammate Jasper Philipsen, a strong sprinter. Van der Poel attacked. Van Aert, who had also just had a puncture, had to chase with Philipsen sitting on his wheel. If van Aert caught van der Poel, Philipsen would win the sprint. If he didn't, van der Poel would win and Philipsen would still come round him for second. Van der Poel won, Philipsen was second and van Aert third.
stories.insight: With two teammates against one rider, the lone rider loses whichever choice he makes. It is the purest illustration of how slipstream and teammates turn a solo effort into a forced loss.
stories.quote: If he doesn't catch him, Van der Poel is winning, and he won't even come second because Philipsen will beat him in the sprint, which is what happens.

stories.topic: Sepp Kuss and the Vuelta gift that split a team
stories.summary: At last year's Vuelta a España, Jumbo-Visma had Primoz Roglic, who had won the Giro and won the Vuelta three times, and Jonas Vingegaard, the reigning Tour champion. Their plan was to put Sepp Kuss, their mountain domestique, into a breakaway and then into the leader's jersey. That would force Remco Evenepoel's Quick-Step team to burn itself out chasing. Instead Evenepoel collapsed and dropped out of contention, leaving Kuss leading with Roglic and Vingegaard second and third. Roglic wanted to race for the win. Social media demanded the team reward Kuss for years of selfless work, and Vingegaard was fine with that. Kuss won, the team took the whole podium, and an angry Roglic left for Bora-Hansgrohe.
stories.insight: Roles inside a team are dynamic, and a plan that works too well can create a crisis of fairness. It also shows public opinion acting on team strategy. Ajay had asked whether riders negotiate before a race; within a team everyone knows their role, but the roles can change mid-race.
stories.quote: for years Sepp Kuss has helped you guys win all these things and this is one moment where you can gift him something beautiful.

stories.topic: Armstrong to Landis: 'Run like you stole something'
stories.summary: In what Amit recalls as Lance Armstrong's last Tour win, his domestique Floyd Landis paced him up the highest mountain of a stage until only four riders were left: Landis, Armstrong, Jan Ullrich and Ivan Basso. Having already gained the time he needed, Armstrong wanted his helper to take the stage on the descent and flat finish. Landis went hard, but the rivals wouldn't let him get away. Armstrong then decided that if Landis couldn't win, he would, and he took the stage himself.
stories.insight: Shows the leader-domestique bargain at work: a leader can try to give his helper a stage win, but the race decides whether the gift is possible.
stories.quote: And Armstrong memorably tells Floyd Landis, run like you stole something because he wants Landis to win now.

stories.topic: Tour de France 2022: Pogacar alone against two Jumbo riders
stories.summary: On a mountain stage over the Col du Galibier finishing on the Col du Granon, Jumbo-Visma had Roglic (secretly too injured from a crash to win) and Vingegaard against defending champion Pogacar. Wout van Aert went up the road in the breakaway and dropped back at the right moment to help his leaders. In the final group of four (Pogacar, Roglic, Vingegaard and a struggling Geraint Thomas), the two Jumbo riders attacked Pogacar in turns, two or three times each. Pogacar decided to attack and try to drop them both. He couldn't shake Vingegaard and spent so much energy that Vingegaard took three minutes on him on the final climb and went on to win the Tour.
stories.insight: Two teammates against one turns every attack into a tax on the lone rider. Amit gives a second explanation too: Pogacar may simply have bonked, or run out of calories. Tactics and nutrition can be equally decisive.
stories.quote: And then Pogacar does something which many people say is profoundly stupid.

stories.topic: How Carapaz won Olympic gold over the strongest rider
stories.summary: Wout van Aert is so powerful that if he reaches the finish with a group, he wins. So rivals, without talking to one another, take turns attacking and leave him to chase each time, which costs him his limited reserves. Peter Sagan suffered the same treatment about ten years earlier. In the last Olympic road race, Richard Carapaz attacked when van Aert was tired of chasing. Nobody else went after him, and Carapaz took gold. Van Aert won silver in the sprint behind and Pogacar took bronze.
stories.insight: The strongest rider in a race can be beaten by rivals who coordinate silently against him. Being the favourite means you are the one who has to chase.
stories.quote: It is just that he is the attacker who Van Aert chose not to follow.

stories.topic: The comeback rider who couldn't keep up
stories.summary: In the late 1980s and early 90s, Greg LeMond, or possibly another top rider (Amit isn't sure), took a few months off. On returning he could barely keep up with the peloton because the pace had become so high. That was a sign something was wrong. Through the 1990s it became a full doping arms race built on EPO, and Tour winners from 1996 for more than a decade were all doping.
stories.insight: From inside a system, a corrupted normal looks normal. It took someone stepping out and coming back to notice how much the baseline had moved.
stories.quote: they took a few months off and then when they got back to the peloton, they could barely keep up with the peloton because the pace was so incredibly high and they realized something is fishy.

stories.topic: Van Aert's sacrifice, wiped out by one crash
stories.summary: Wout van Aert, a cyclocross world champion, skipped this year's cyclocross world championship and spent weeks at high altitude to target the cobbled classics, the Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix. Around the first big cobbled monument he had a terrible crash through no fault of his own and was out for weeks. Pogacar had a similar year earlier: a fall at Liège-Bastogne-Liège about six weeks before the Tour de France disrupted his training, and he couldn't really compete for the Tour.
stories.insight: Modern cycling plans training with scientific precision, which makes luck all the crueller. Months of optimisation can disappear in one fall.
stories.quote: He skipped everything before that. Big sacrifice.

stories.topic: Roglic: from a skiing crash to an unfinished redemption story
stories.summary: As a teenager in a junior skiing championship, the Slovenian Primoz Roglic had a horrific crash, which Amit still rewatches. He skied again but realised he wouldn't be among the world's best, so he took up cycling late. Some say that is why he isn't a great bike handler. He became one of the great riders of his generation and won the Vuelta three times. His Tour de France luck has been brutal: lost to Pogacar in 2020, knocked out by a crash (Sonny Colbrelli took him down) in 2021, injured by a crash in 2022, and passed over in favour of Vingegaard in 2023, when he went to the Giro and won it. He then left for Bora-Hansgrohe.
stories.insight: Late starts and forced changes of direction can still produce greatness. Following sport means following arcs like this one, which hasn't yet had its ending.
stories.quote: But he says that I love sport, man. I just love sport. I want to go out there, I want to compete, I want to be physical.

stories.topic: Pogacar's 2020 time trial and the myth that Roglic collapsed
stories.summary: In the Covid year of 2020, Roglic led the Tour going into the decisive penultimate-day time trial. He hadn't bothered attacking the 21-year-old Pogacar, who was in second place, because he didn't see him as a threat. Roglic was a great time trialist and the current Olympic champion in the event. He started last and kept hearing on the radio that Pogacar was going faster. By the final climb his teammates, van Aert among them, could see the dream was over. Pogacar won the stage and the Tour. Amit tweeted at the time that it was one of the seminal moments in world sport. Afterwards the 30-year-old Roglic went over to shake Pogacar's hand and hug him.
stories.insight: The popular story is that Roglic collapsed, and Amit says it's false. Roglic rode a strong time trial and was beaten by something extraordinary. Keep a loser's performance separate from the outcome.
stories.quote: Roglic came fifth in the stage out of hundred and fifty people. He did a great time trial. But Pogacar was just on another fucking planet.

stories.topic: Evenepoel's revenge on his own teammate
stories.summary: At the world championships and the Olympics, riders race for national teams. As a young rider, Remco Evenepoel was told to work for his fellow Belgian Wout van Aert, the favourite in a world championship road race. He worked hard, but van Aert didn't have the legs that day, and Evenepoel was furious, believing he could have won. The next year Evenepoel attacked alone. Van Aert, as his teammate, couldn't chase him, so he stayed with the others. Nobody caught Evenepoel and he became world champion.
stories.insight: Team rules that hold you back one year can carry you the next. Rivalries inside a team can matter as much as rivalries between teams.
stories.quote: And once he goes off on a breakaway, uh, you know, Wout van Aert cannot follow him because teammate.

recommendations.creator: Chris Froome
recommendations.context: In the recommendations chapter Amit said there are many great cycling books and named only this one before turning to YouTube channels.
recommendations.reason: He calls it great. Froome was the rider Team Sky's 'Sky Train' was built around, a strategy discussed at length in the episode.

recommendations.creator: Chris Horner
recommendations.context: Amit's first main recommendation. Horner is the oldest man to win a grand tour, having won the Vuelta a España at 41.
recommendations.reason: After every stage of a major race Horner gives his own analysis and calls teams 'knuckleheads' for wasting energy, joining pointless breakaways or failing to chase. While tearing into other commentators he teaches real tactical and strategic thinking, and Amit says he just makes you a better thinker.

recommendations.item: The BIGGEST Day of My Career (Chris Horner on his Vuelta a España win)
recommendations.creator: Chris Horner
recommendations.context: Amit mentioned that Horner has videos on how he won the Vuelta at 41 and promised to link them.
recommendations.reason: The winner's own account of how a 41-year-old won a grand tour.

recommendations.creator: Patrick and Benji
recommendations.context: Amit's second YouTube recommendation, run by two young enthusiasts. Amit believes Patrick also consults on strategy for Visma-Lease a Bike.
recommendations.reason: They do hour-long deep dives after races and detailed previews, which gives a different dimension from Horner. For Amit, following a sport means taking in everything around the racing and 'expanding your brain' in the process.

recommendations.context: Amit guessed the Lanterne Rouge Tour preview would already be up for the race's start and promised to link it.
recommendations.reason: A ready-made briefing on the contenders and storylines for anyone starting to watch the 2024 Tour.

recommendations.context: After GCN Plus was sold and stopped being available in India, Amit suggested subscribing to Eurosport with your location set to England.
recommendations.reason: One of his great joys of watching cycling was the commentary of Dan Lloyd, Orla Chennaoui and Adam Blythe, and he thinks they're on Eurosport now.

recommendations.context: Amit couldn't find a way to watch cycling in India without a VPN.
recommendations.reason: He uses it himself and says any good VPN works. It's the practical route to Eurosport or other geo-restricted race coverage.

recommendations.context: Amit said his chess episode was 'just like this' one: a sport explained by a passionate fan.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit contrasted it with this episode.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentioned that he teaches his writing students Dave Brailsford's idea of the aggregation of marginal gains.
recommendations.reason: His own writing course, where he applies ideas like marginal gains to the craft of writing.

core_ideas.concept: You don't have to be a hen to know about eggs
core_ideas.explanation: Amit can't ride a cycle, yet the whole episode is a close analysis of the sport. Ajay's maxim, which Amit credits to him, says deep understanding doesn't require being a practitioner, and that being inside a thing can even get in the way of seeing it clearly.
core_ideas.quote: You don't have to be a hen to know about eggs. In fact, being a hen is an impediment to knowing about eggs.

core_ideas.explanation: Road cycling is several contests. One-day classics run five to seven hours and 150 to 250 km; the five most prestigious are called monuments. Some are hilly, some cobbled, and Milan-San Remo is mostly flat with decisive late hills. Time trials pit one rider against the clock, and taking another rider's slipstream gets you disqualified, so they come down to aerodynamics and pacing. One-week stage races such as Paris-Nice, Tirreno-Adriatico, the Tour of the Basque Country and the Tour of Switzerland mix stage types. The three-week grand tours (Giro, Tour, Vuelta) combine flats, hills and brutal mountaintop finishes and become tests of endurance and character.
core_ideas.quote: by the time you're ending one of these grand tours, you can see it on the faces and their bodies, and it becomes a test of pure character.

core_ideas.concept: Body weight decides what kind of rider you are
core_ideas.explanation: Because power-to-weight ratio dominates on long climbs, grand-tour contenders like Pogacar, Vingegaard, Roglic and Evenepoel weigh around 60 to 65 kg. Climbing is non-negotiable for them, but they must also time-trial well. Heavier riders, up to the late 70s in kg (van Aert, van der Poel, earlier Sagan), are puncheurs: explosive on flats, cobbles and short steep climbs, which suits the one-day classics. Sprinters with fast-twitch muscles are protected all day and then explode over the last few dozen metres. Riders who don't excel at any of these become domestiques. Amit's one exception, the heavier Lance Armstrong, raced in the drug era.
core_ideas.quote: If you are a lighter rider, you are likely to be a better climber.

core_ideas.concept: Different jerseys, different games on the same road
core_ideas.explanation: The general classification (yellow at the Tour) goes to the lowest total time over three weeks. The points classification (green) rewards stage results and intermediate sprints, so sprinters chase it and ignore overall time. There are also a mountains jersey and, at the Tour, a white jersey for the best rider under 25. A sprinter losing an hour on a mountain stage isn't failing; he's playing a different game.
core_ideas.quote: I will lose one hour on a particular stage. I don't give a shit. I just want to optimize for those stages where I can do well.

core_ideas.concept: The slipstream is what makes cycling a team sport
core_ideas.explanation: A rider directly behind another sits in a pocket of low air pressure and saves about 30% of the effort. So the riders you see on screen are not working equally. Teams of around eight shelter their leader, with each domestique riding in front until exhausted and then peeling off for the next. Nearly every tactic in the sport follows from this one fact of physics.
core_ideas.quote: That all the people that you see on the screen who are cycling are not putting in equal effort. It is the guys who are out on the wind who are putting in that effort, and the people behind them are not.

core_ideas.concept: Cooperation between rivals in a breakaway
core_ideas.explanation: A lone rider can't stay away for long because he is always in the wind, so rival riders in a breakaway take turns at the front without speaking. Ajay calls it informal coordination. Sitting on the back without working is frowned on, except for tactical reasons: a teammate is the favourite in the group behind, or a stronger climber waits for you on a hill in exchange for you doing more work on the flat. The cooperation ends as the finish nears.
core_ideas.quote: Typically it is considered desperately uncool to be a cheater and only sit in the slipstream.

core_ideas.concept: How the peloton manages a breakaway
core_ideas.explanation: Teams that want to win, whether sprinters' teams on flat stages or climbers' teams on hilly ones, send rouleurs to the front of the peloton. Each of them only has to last about 20 km, so they can ride harder than breakaway riders who must last 100 km. They hold the gap at around three minutes and plan the catch late, because catching the break too early invites new attacks. Rival sprint teams play chicken over who does the chasing, which sometimes lets the breakaway survive. On some days GC teams deliberately let harmless breakaways go.
core_ideas.quote: These fuckers are taking a free roll, they'll have more people at the end. We don't want that to happen.

core_ideas.concept: Why nobody wants to lead a sprint
core_ideas.explanation: A sprinter wants to leave the slipstream as late as possible. Strong teams build lead-out trains to deliver him there; riders without one try to latch onto another sprinter's lead-out. At the end of a breakaway this produces a stand-off in which riders slow almost to a halt and watch one another, because whoever leads usually loses. The stand-off can let chasers catch up, as at Flanders in 2022.
core_ideas.quote: all things being equal, the guy in front is guaranteed to lose because they will come out of his slipstream.

core_ideas.explanation: Each rider has only so many hard efforts in him. When someone attacks from a small group, everyone wants someone else to chase. Two teammates can attack in turns until a lone rival runs out of efforts, as Jumbo did to Pogacar and van der Poel and Philipsen did to van Aert. The same logic lets a field beat the strongest rider without any agreement: they keep attacking and leave him to chase each time.
core_ideas.quote: Because whoever spends energy chasing the first guy down will not have the energy to win in the end. You have limited bullets.

core_ideas.concept: The Sky Train: pace-setting as a weapon
core_ideas.explanation: First US Postal and later Team Sky (for Chris Froome) controlled races by setting a relentless pace instead of attacking. Their rouleurs wore themselves out on the flats at a speed nobody could attack from, then their mountain domestiques kept it high on the climbs. The peloton stretches from a triangle into a single line, rivals lose their teammates, and the leader reaches the final climb with helpers still around him while his rivals are alone.
core_ideas.quote: Beyond a certain pace, no one can jump away from you. The acceleration and power required is too much.

core_ideas.explanation: Put a capable domestique into a breakaway and into the race lead. The rival team then has to spend its riders' energy chasing him while your real leaders rest in the peloton, ready to attack once the rival's team is worn out. Jumbo-Visma tried this with Sepp Kuss at the 2023 Vuelta. It worked so well that the decoy won the race.
core_ideas.quote: Remco Evenepoel and his team can't waste energy chasing someone who's not a contender.

core_ideas.concept: Strategy before the race, tactics during it
core_ideas.explanation: Teams plan strategy months and days in advance, then adjust tactics in real time. Every rider is on the radio, and a directeur sportif in the team car watches the TV feed and live power data and calls the moves. Training data, sometimes visible on Strava, shows how teams prepare. Amit describes cycling as short-term chess inside long-term chess.
core_ideas.quote: So you have strategy, which you decide before a race, and then you have tactics which you decide during the race.

core_ideas.explanation: Running out of calories, called bonking, can wreck a race regardless of fitness or tactics. Riders must keep eating throughout, the directeur sportif reminds them when to eat, and part of a domestique's job is to drop back to the team car, stuff his jersey with bars and drinks, and carry them up to the leaders.
core_ideas.quote: In fact, a good directeur sportif in the car will keep informing you that you need to eat now, you need to eat now.

core_ideas.concept: The doping arms race, and why to watch in good faith now
core_ideas.explanation: From the late 1980s, and especially through the 1990s, cycling became a drug arms race built on EPO, which mimics the red-blood-cell benefits of altitude training. To compete at all you had to dope, so singling out one villain misses the point. The authorities declared whole years of results void, including all seven of Armstrong's wins, rather than passing titles down to the next finisher. Since the early 2010s better testing and teams policing their own riders have, in Amit's view, made the sport largely clean. Today's high speeds come from better training science.
core_ideas.quote: I would say watch it in good faith.

core_ideas.explanation: Dave Brailsford took British cycling from the bottom of the heap, and Team Sky went on to win the Tour de France seven times in eight years. There was no single breakthrough. He looked for 1% improvements in everything: diet, training plan, riding position, helmet aerodynamics. Amit teaches the idea to his writing students. Brailsford is now Jim Ratcliffe's right-hand man in the effort to turn Manchester United around.
core_ideas.quote: His insight was you don't need one big improvement. You look at a bunch of different things, like what is your diet. What is your training plan? What is your position on the cycle? How aerodynamic is your helmet? And you improve one percent on each of them, and you keep looking for one percent improvements. And that aggregation of marginal gains will take you to a whole different place.

core_ideas.concept: Luck is part of the sport
core_ideas.explanation: Crashes usually happen because one wheel touches another and riders go down like dominoes. Even perfect preparation can't protect you: Vingegaard, Roglic and Evenepoel all crashed together at this year's Tour of the Basque Country weeks before the Tour. Teams try to reduce the risk by keeping their leader near the front of the peloton.
core_ideas.quote: which is why what teams in grand tours will do is they'll try to keep their man towards the front because the more towards the front you are, the less chance of getting caught up in a domino effect of a bike fall.

core_ideas.concept: We follow sport for the stories
core_ideas.explanation: Beyond physical extremes, sport holds us through rivalries and redemption arcs: Roglic's unfinished quest for the Tour, Pogacar against Vingegaard, the Belgian tension between Evenepoel and van Aert, and van Aert against van der Poel, Belgium against Holland, a rivalry that began in cyclocross. These turn three weeks of racing into a drama.
core_ideas.quote: we follow sport not just to see the limits of human achievement, but we get caught up in the stories of the people who are involved. We care about key rivalries, we care about redemption tales

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay opens the episode: 'Amit, tell me, you look like a guy who would be very fast on a cycle.' Amit: 'This is really a low blow. And you know, the Bengali in me does not appreciate this low blow.' Later, explaining why you'd never see him on a real cricket field: 'I'm Bengali. Have some peace.'
Amit, a former managing editor of Cricinfo, lists the sports he follows closely: 'One is chess, and cricket is not one of the other ones, by the way.'
After Amit clean-bowled Rahul Dravid twice with a trick office-cricket ball, Dravid threw the bat away: 'Fuck you, Shoaib Akhtar, I'm not playing with you.'

Amit, who took local trains and buses for years before buying a car: 'I am now the best driver in Bombay. Because driving in Bombay is not about driving, it is about Bombay. But that is a subject for another episode.'
Right after Ajay's 'You don't have to be a hen to know about eggs', Amit: 'Welcome to a scrambled eggs episode on cycling.'
While defining a breakaway, Amit to Ajay: 'In a sense, when it comes to mainstream economics, you are a breakaway, and the peloton is far, far, far behind you.'

Before explaining slipstream, Amit checks Ajay's credentials: 'Are you a card carrying physicist? Also an aeronautical engineer.' The running gag returns when Amit tells young men to save their energy for 'economics and physics and aeronautical engineering and all the other things that this man is a card holding member of.'

Ajay claims childhood cycling glory for riding up a slope and round a curve with both hands off. Amit: 'Had you been French or Belgian... the loss of economics could have been the gain of cycling.' Ajay: 'Yeah, this is why economic development matters.'

Amit's VPN advisory: 'Just for this reason, I don't want you to get a VPN. Young men watching this for porn, okay? Do not do that. It is sinful, save your energy for studying economics and physics and aeronautical engineering.'
Chris Horner's favourite word for teams that waste energy or chase at the wrong time: 'knuckleheads.'
The peloton, the main pack of riders, is where Amit thinks the fitness brand Peloton got its name.

Milan-San Remo, one of the five cycling monuments, is nicknamed La Primavera because it is held in spring. Alpe d'Huez is the famous Tour de France mountaintop finish that separates great climbers from good ones.
Cycling's vocabulary comes from French because the French pioneered European cycling: domestique (the helper), directeur sportif (the tactician in the team car), puncheur (the explosive rider).

Ajay compares cycling teams' live rider data to professional basketball, where he has read that players are instrumented so coaches can watch their VO2 max and substitute tired players. Amit notes cyclists can't be substituted.

Doping parallels: Ajay compares cycling's doping to the testing arms race around Russian and Chinese athletes at the Olympics. Amit hopes cycling is now as clean as cricket after its match-fixing dark age.
Amit on why cycling is a pure test of the body: 'It's not like Formula One where the car matters so much.'
